# Sallowmere Reach

*A NovaForge novel*

## Synopsis

Ada Rowe has spent eleven years keeping a book that isn't quite true. As keeper of the Corbie Light, she alone may write in the Register of Passage, and only within the hour of a sighting — but a sighting, by the letter of the rule, includes a petition carried up from the drowned street below, where the Ridge households leave the names of boats no return will ever confirm. So Ada copies the dead onto the page as if they still passed the light, one line at a time, in ink that cannot be struck out. It is not quite forgery. It is not quite mercy, either.

One name stands twice already: the *Marigold*, entered by the keeper before her, an hour that does not fit the tide that drowned him with it. A third entry would close the name forever — and Nell Harker, who has left a petition on the seventh step at every low water for nine years, wants nothing else. But closure means admission, and admission is what Thomas Creed's spring-tide audit is built to punish. Then, the night before the Commissioners arrive to make the book agree with the sea, a new line appears on page 91, written in a hand that drowned eleven years ago. Ada must decide whether to let it stand, knowing what the Register does to a name entered three times — and what it costs the keeper who writes it.

For readers of *The Little Stranger* and *Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell*.

---

# Chapter 1 — The Seventh Step

The water went off the causeway at twenty past two and Ada Rowe went down the stair behind it, one hand on the wet rope, counting steps she had not needed to count in eleven years.

Three petitions on the seventh step. Two weighted with stones, one with a scrap of net float, grey, the twine gone to fur.

Nell Harker stood four steps below with her boots in the standing water and did not come up. She never had. She looked at the papers in Ada's hand and then out at the shoal, where the Reach lay flat and brown and the drowned street showed its gable ends.

"Low water again tomorrow," Ada said.

"If it's written," Nell said.

Ada climbed. Behind her the stair dripped and the Corbie Light stood unlit above it, waiting on the sun.

In the lamp room she laid the three papers out and read them in the order she had lifted them. A hand she knew: *Sweet Providence, smack, lost off the Ness, my grandfather's.* She wiped the nib on the inside of her left cuff, which was black to the elbow and had been for years, and wrote: *2.41, east by north, Sweet Providence, smack.* Iron-gall, one line, the hour of the sighting and the hour of the writing the same hour. She read it back. It stood.

The second she entered likewise. The third she did not.

The third said *Marigold* in Nell Harker's square, patient letters, and Ada set it flat at the desk's edge with the net float on it and left it there, unwritten, as she had left it every low water for two years.

Thomas Creed came up the causeway at four with his case under his arm and salt to his knees. He took the last quarter's returns out and went down the unmatched names at half voice, the way he did everything — "*Sweet Providence*, no return; *Kestrel*, no return; *Ann Bligh*, no return" — and stopped when she set the cup down beside him, and started the column again from the top.

"Spring tide in two days," he said. "Dawn of the sixteenth. I'll audit the book page by page and the oil against the hours."

"It'll be open."

"Mistress Rowe." He squared the returns. "The *Marigold* stands twice in that book. Enter her a third time and she goes to the Drowned Page, and I will countersign her there myself, and the name is closed. Never entered again. Not by you, not by anyone after you."

Ada looked at the water beginning to feel its way back along the causeway, filling the ruts first.

"You'd best go down," she said, "while there's road."

He went. The flood took the stones behind him a length at a time, and by the time he reached the Ridge there was no causeway, only the Reach, and the seventh step under two feet of it.

The petition lay flat on the desk under its net float. The name on it stood nowhere in the book. The tide clock went on and on, louder than the sea.

# Chapter 2 — A Hand Not Mine

At sunset Ada Rowe set the character: two flashes and a dark, every half minute, the clockwork wound and the oil topped and the glass wiped free of salt. She stood the first hours of the watch with nothing passing. Then, with Creed's audit falling at dawn on the sixteenth, she took the Register down from its shelf, meaning to set Walter Byrd's first entry beside her own, and turned back to page 91.

Beneath Walter Byrd's entry there was a new line on the page, and by the rule a line in a hand not the keeper's counts toward nothing at all.

*Three of the clock, sou'-sou'-west, Marigold, ketch.* Squared, backward-leaning, the hour written out in full where she would have written 3.00. The ink was iron-gall and it was dry. The page had been clear beneath that entry when she closed the book at the turn of the tide; she was certain of it the way she was certain of the stair under her feet.

She did not touch it. No entry may be struck out, and a line in a hand not the keeper's voids the whole page. What the rule required was not judgement but labour: recopy the page entire, the offending line with the rest, carry the copy down to the seventh step, have it signed there by two Ridge witnesses before the next high water. She set the book open, weighted the leaf, and went to fetch a clean sheet.

Behind her the lamp lost its character.

She counted. The dark held past a full minute. Ada went out to the Causeway Bell and rang it, without pause, her arm going and going while the weather came off the water, until the clockwork caught and the two flashes and the dark came back over the drowned street.

Somebody was on the stair. Nell Harker came up out of the dark to the seventh step and no further, her shawl black with spray.

"The *Marigold* stands written on page 91," Ada called down. "In a hand that is not mine."

"If it's written," Nell said. And then, into the wind: "The *Marigold*."

Eleven years, and the name gone out of her at last.

Ada went up and wrote. She wiped the nib on the inside of her cuff before every line and copied page 91 entire, every vessel, every bearing, and then the line she had not made — *three of the clock, sou'-sou'-west, Marigold, ketch* — in her own upright hand, the hour in words because the copy must be faithful.

Before high water she carried the fair copy down to the seventh step and no further. Nell Harker signed, and another from the Ridge signed beneath her, the stone wet under the paper.

Ada held the sheet flat against the spray. The *Marigold* stood in her own handwriting, as it had these nine years, but for the first time in a line she had not composed.

# Chapter 3 — The Drowned Page

Creed came up at first light with the returns under his arm, and Ada put the Light out at sunrise and opened the Register on the desk for him. He read at half voice as he wrote: four gallons against fourteen hours burned, five against seventeen, the numbers going down his column like water finding its level. Two valid entries of the *Marigold* stood in the book, Walter Byrd's of eleven years ago and her own of nine. The line that had come in the night counted toward nothing and had been recopied and witnessed at the step. Ada stood with her left cuff black to the elbow and let him count.

At page 91 he stopped mid-sum. He put one finger below the squared, backward-leaning hand with the hour written in full, and asked her where the names came from that he could not match to any return.

"Off the seventh step," Ada said. "The petitions. I copy the name and enter it within the hour, in my hand, at a bearing I choose."

"Every one of them."

"Every one." She offered nothing after it.

Creed laid his own return beside the page and smoothed it flat. The *Marigold* had sailed at ten of the clock on the third of March. Walter's line gave three of the clock that same morning, nineteen hours before. At the turn of the tide Ada read both aloud in the lamp room, the hour on the page and the hour on the return, because that was the hour this place read things aloud in, and nothing else could be done with two times that could not both be true, and the sound of them went out into the salt and did not come back with anything. Creed did not offer a reason. Neither did she. They stood in it a moment, and then it was simply read, and standing.

Ada took up the pen and wiped the nib on the inside of her cuff. Nell Harker's petition had come up with this morning's low water, as one did at every low water, and it was in Ada's hand already, the scrap of net float knotted through it, the same asking refused for two years; she copied it out within the hour: *Marigold, ketch, sou'-sou'-west.* The third. Then she turned to the back of the book, to the Drowned Page, and wrote the name there herself, because no other hand might. Creed took the pen from her and countersigned beneath the line. It cost him. She watched it cost him, a vessel he could match to nothing at all, and he wrote his name under her anyway rather than leave it open.

She carried the book down to the head of the stair. Nell stood on the seventh step and did not climb, and Ada read the Drowned Page line down to her, the name and the date and the countersignature, while the chimneys of the drowned street came up out of the ebb below them.

"*Marigold*," Nell said, once, aloud, over the water.

Ada shut the Register. She wiped a clean nib on her cuff, out of habit, on a cuff that would never write that word again.
